You tip hot water over a handful of leaves. Steam rises. The water darkens—maybe green-gold, maybe deep amber—and a smell fills the room that is somehow both sharp and soft. Twenty minutes later you are a little more awake. Sometimes you also feel a little calmer. Coffee can wake you up too. So why does *tea* so often feel like a different kind of alertness?

That question is the door into this site.

This is not a lab notebook and not a sales brochure. It is a **story-shaped journey** through a drink that almost everyone has tried and almost nobody fully explains. The facts come from owner-supplied source packs, and—where we expand a chapter—from peer-reviewed papers, historical archives, and university pages we opened and checked. The owner of this site is an economist. We do **not** invent economic theories here. We only retell what those sources already support—in plain English a smart high-school student can follow.

Each **lesson** is meant to be long enough to be interesting and short enough to stay a story. **Clickable footnotes** work both ways (tap the number → source; tap the caret → back to the sentence; hover often shows a popup). Denser study tables and side-stories sit in collapsed **"More detail…"** foldouts so the open page does not feel like a wall of text. The [Bibliography](bibliography.qmd) remains the master map across the whole site.

## What this journey is about

Think of four chapters that follow one continuous thread—each with **four lessons** matching the source-pack branches.

First you meet the **leaf**—where tea comes from, why green and black look so different, what brewing pulls into the mug, and three headline compounds. Then you follow those compounds **into the body**: brain signaling, brain-wave patterns, stress hormones, and quiet body signals. Next you zoom out. Tea remade **trade balances**, became a monastic focus aid, and even a warm mug in the hand shows up in experiments on trust. A short brewing break can also act as a practical stress reset. Finally you ask the decision question: do drinks **nudge** how fast we answer, how much risk we take, how much we care about tomorrow, and how trusting we are in a first move?

You can start anywhere. But if you read in order, each lesson hands you a reason to open the next.

## How to travel with this site

When a number appears—say "about 30–50 mg caffeine"—treat it as a **typical range from the packs**, not a promise about your exact mug. Brands, leaves, and steep times differ. The [Cup reference](cup-reference.qmd) is the quick table for a common 250 mL cup.

New to grocery and cafe labels? Start with **[Tea basics](tea-basics.qmd)** before or alongside Chapter 1.

When a technical word appears, we define it in the story the first time. The [Glossary](glossary.qmd) is there when you want a one-line reminder (with links into the right chapter hub).

When you wonder how a brewing fact connects to mood, or a warm mug to a trust game, open [Linkages](linkages.qmd). Those eleven bridges sew the chapters together.

When you want the paper behind a name-and-year—or a footnote marker on a lesson page—click the footnote or open the [Bibliography](bibliography.qmd).

## What we refuse to invent

We do **not** invent new percentages, mechanisms, history figures, or study results. We do **not** paste walls of lab equations. Everything here should trace back to the verified packs or a source we opened and listed. That honesty is part of the story: curiosity without costume jewelry.

Ready? Pour an imaginary cup—and start with [Tea basics](tea-basics.qmd) if labels feel confusing, then [Chapter 1: The Chemical Core](modules/module-01/index.qmd)—or skim the [roadmap](modules/index.qmd) first.
